title: Checkpoint: Where Philosophy Began
objective: After this level you can compare how Greek, Chinese and Indian thinkers first asked what is real and how to live.
summary: Greek thinkers asked what is most real (Forms or form in things), Chinese thinkers how to live and govern, and Indian schools argued over the self.

cards.headline: Chapter 1 finale: three places, two big questions.
cards.body: What is real? How should you live? Greek, Chinese and Indian thinkers gave very different first answers, and argued over the self. Line them up.

items.label: Greece
points: Plato: the most real are Forms, known by thought
Aristotle: form lives in things, like the bronze statue’s shape

items.label: China
points: Confucius: become a junzi through ren and li
Laozi: follow the Dao and act like water

items.label: India
points: Buddhists: no lasting self, only changing parts
Advaita: the self is one with Brahman

cards.headline: Rulers were listening
cards.body: Chinese philosophers spoke to rulers as well as to individuals. Training in li was part of preparing rulers and officials. Even the Daodejing gives political advice: when the sage governs through non-action, it says, good order is universal. How to live and how to rule came as a pair.

cards.headline: The self on trial
cards.body: India’s schools argued hardest about the self. Buddhist philosophers found only impermanent parts, a person named the way a chariot is. Nyaya thinkers insisted memory needs an enduring self. Advaita Vedanta went the other way entirely: your self is identical with Brahman, the reality under everything. One question, three incompatible answers, each defended with arguments.

cards.headline: Chapter 1 complete
learned: How Greek, Chinese and Indian thinkers first asked what is real and how to live.
What philosophy is, and why it answers its questions with arguments, not only experiments.
How a thought experiment such as Galileo’s tied balls or Gyges’s ring tests an idea.
Why Buddhist philosophers compared a person to a chariot, and how their critics replied.

questions.prompt: What one thing does Glaucon’s ring of invisibility remove from the test?

options.label: The difference between rich and poor

questions.explanation: The ring removes only the chance of being caught, so it tests whether people are just only out of fear.

questions.prompt: The natural image the Daodejing uses as its model for wu wei is _____.

options.label: fire
options.rationale: The model is soft and yielding.

options.label: a mountain
options.rationale: The model is soft and yielding.

options.label: lightning
options.rationale: The model is soft and yielding.

questions.explanation: Water benefits all things without striving, yet nothing beats it against the hard and strong.

questions.prompt: How did Advaita Vedanta’s view of the self differ from the Buddhist no-self view?

options.label: Both denied any self at all
Advaita identified the self with Brahman instead of denying it
Advaita said the self is just the body
Buddhists, not Advaita, said the self is identical with Brahman
options.rationale: That’s the Advaita view, not the Buddhist one.

questions.explanation: Buddhist philosophers found no lasting self; Advaita held that the individual self is identical with Brahman.

questions.prompt: Whom besides individuals did early Chinese philosophers address?
questions.explanation: Training in li prepared rulers and officials, and the Daodejing advises the sage who governs through non-action.

questions.prompt: Match each thinker or school with its answer to a big question.

pairs.right: Become a junzi through ren and li
Follow the Dao and act like water
The self is one with Brahman

questions.explanation: Plato said the most real things are Forms, Confucius said become a junzi through ren and li, Laozi said follow the Dao and act like water, and Advaita said the self is one with Brahman.
